To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(1) the radiation-induced damage to protein crystal is caused by a complex interplay of different effects, including (a) the formation of radical species, (b) the generation of heat, (c) the production of free radicals, and (d) the formation of covalent bonds; (2) the damage is dependent on the crystallographic unit cell, the crystal size, the temperature of measurement, the dose rate and the presence of potential scavenger species; (3)

radiation damage to protein crystals is due to free radicals formed in the protein and the solvent, that the damage is reduced when scavenger molecules are present and that it is increased when the crystal is irradiated at room temperature rather than at cryo-temperature.
the radiation-damage process in proteins is initiated by the generation of free radicals.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the study of the effects of X-rays on biological macromolecules.
the effects of radiation damage in biological macromolecular crystals, particularly those of proteins and DNA.
the development and application of techniques to measure the radiation damage induced by X-rays in protein crystals.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the radiation damage is a function of dose, temperature, solvent, pH, crystal size, crystal shape and the presence of scavenger molecules.
radiation damage to protein crystals is caused by free radicals, which are produced by ionisation and are scavenged by the solvent and by other molecules present.
the radiation damage in protein crystallography is due to a combination of direct and indirect effects.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
radiation damage in proteins can be reduced by lowering the temperature and by the presence of scavenger molecules.
, at cryo-tempeatures, radiation damage to proteins is caused primarily by the production of free radicals.

the damage to a protein crystal is a complex process involving many different factors, but the most important is probably the formation of radicals, which are then scavenged by the solvent and/or the protein molecules.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the damage is a result of a complex process which can be described by a series of stages.

radiation damage is not a simple, linear process, but rather a complex, non-linear process that depends on the structure of the crystal, its temperature, its hydration state, and the presence of scavenger molecules.
radiation damage is a complex process and that the damage to the crystal structure and the protein molecule are not necessarily correlated.
